extracted.intended_audience: computer science and mathematics researchers, graduate students, and technical authors writing papers, books, and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing clear, ethical, and effective academic writing in computer science and mathematics — covering papers, books, proofs, examples, notation, and style. Emphasis on what makes publications appropriate for different venues and how to improve exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coping with competition / Know the market and yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the market, know thyself, and work out a compromise of your own. Don’t slavishly imitate another’s style, but don’t avoid it either. Don’t hesitate to follow the crowd when they are all going in the right direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of prevailing practices in introductory texts and courses; adapt them to your strengths rather than copying purely for novelty. Balance originality with recognizability for the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism standard / when imitation becomes culpable
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation ceases to be flattery and becomes culpable if a reasonable person could not believe that you didn’t have the other chap’s book open in front of you as you wrote yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot copyright ideas, only expressions — but verbatim copying of text, equations, notation, or distinctive formatting (e.g., identical italics usage) can be damning. Be explicit in quotations and acknowledge sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation practices for surveys and papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey papers will often contain verbatim quotes; there’s no problem since the writer is not presenting the work as his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when quoting in surveys, be explicit about quotations and attributions; accusations of plagiarism often hinge on presentation and (perceived) financial loss, so clarity helps avoid misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edition management / reusing material
rubrics_metrics.description: Second and subsequent editions still consume substantial time but go faster if you can use earlier examples; new editions restart sales cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuse earlier examples prudently for new editions to save time, but ensure updates correct errors and reflect new understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poor motives for publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two bad reasons to write a paper: (1) to have a long publications list; (2) to have a paper published in a specific conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't publish merely for CV padding or to appear in particular proceedings; such motives can lead to sloppy work and diminished integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish for a good reason: genuine excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: You should publish when 'You have done something that you are excited about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let genuine contribution and enthusiasm motivate publication; quality-driven reasons produce better papers than careerist ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to write by reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to write is more like learning to play the piano than like learning to type; you learn by reading—read great literature as well as technical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplary writers (both technical and literary) to internalize structure, rhythm, and craft; reading broadly sharpens style and critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad thinking produces bad writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad writing comes from bad thinking, and bad thinking never produces good writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clarity of understanding before polishing prose; fix ideas first, then sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate publication venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal articles should be polished and timeless; conference papers can be a little rougher and suit work 'not yet ready for the archives'; technical reports are for work not ready for broad distribution but worth writing up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match venue to readiness and permanence of results; remember technical reports may later become journal articles and will still have readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conceits/themes sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceit (a fanciful idea around which a paper can be built) can catalyze writing but should be abandoned if it intrudes; the line between useful conceit and merely cute is fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jokes and fleeting playfulness that date poorly; use metaphors only if they aid long-term clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer examples to abstract dry exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to have one solid example than to have a dry, abstract, academic paper; simple examples are rarely a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, sometimes very simple examples to illustrate concepts; they keep you honest and reveal limitations of your claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix ideas before fixing sentences or format
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing concern that people often 'fix the sentence and not the idea'; don't think about formatting when writing—do think about structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on conceptual structure first; defer formatting details until the exposition is conceptually sound. Use macros to hide notation complexity while drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and algebra as tools for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebra has provided a tool for presenting the structure of a formula; we can improve practice by making the structure of an entire discourse more clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise notation and structural aids to reveal relationships; consider notation trends and redesign presentation to expose structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured/tabular proofs to clarify reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabular 'statement–reason' proofs (like high-school geometry style) are much easier to read and can help clarify proofs presented in paragraph style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tabular forms during drafting to enforce clear logical structure; then convert to readable paragraph proofs with the same clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentence should leap and be nontechnical
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence can be expected to be nontechnical and to represent an author’s best effort; you should be excited about what you are writing and that excitement should show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a direct, simple, nonpassive opening that grabs attention; do not let subsequent sentences fall short of the promise of the opener.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive 'wimpiness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid passive wimpiness; be simple and direct—'Get right down to business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active voice and assertive phrasing to make claims and narrative clearer and stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain writing energy through the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you hit readers in the gut with your first sentence, you can’t let them down with your second—by induction, maintain momentum throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain engaging, clear writing from start to finish; avoid sections that sag or lose the reader's interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Write, rewrite, rewrite, rewrite… Almost all good work requires substantial labor over multiple drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to discard many early drafts; revision is essential to clarity and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get critical feedback and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let anything you write be published without having had others critique it; a university environment is good for feedback but timing matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek knowledgeable reviewers, peers, or students to find logical errors and weaknesses before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach material while writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to teach a course on a topic at the time you are writing it up—teaching helps discipline exposition and reveals misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lectures and student questions as a testbed for clarity; revise manuscript based on teaching experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read broadly and continually
rubrics_metrics.description: Read a great deal; it sharpens your style and gets your critical faculties working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both technical literature and great literature to learn structure, rhythm, and expressive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the reader and anticipate misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself what the reader’s primitives are; 'How is the reader going to misunderstand me here?' Develop internal 'daemons' to catch errors automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train habits that flag common problems (e.g., split infinitives, ambiguous references) so you catch them without conscious checklisting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the medium (vocabulary, graphs, typography)
rubrics_metrics.description: You need a good vocabulary (not necessarily many big words) and mastery of other mediums like graphs, indexes, tables, and typography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate visual aids and typographic conventions (e.g., typewriter font for logical formulae) to convey distinctions and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the material via writing and reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing reorganizes internal models; the act of composing forces understanding and can reveal errors in your thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use writing, lectures, and talks to test and refine your internal model; accept that writing helps you learn what you mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify exposition; use the 80-20 rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the reader with something straightforward first; use simple examples to convey most of the point (80% truth with 20% difficulty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify initially, and later add correct details and generalizations; don't shy from starting with simplified models for exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling old material without revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the temptation to reuse old material verbatim; new context usually demands rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite previously published passages to fit the new emphasis, audience, and updated knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep shooting for perfection even if you’ll never reach it; demand the best in everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain high standards in clarity, correctness, and presentation; incremental improvements matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length targets and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for an average sentence length under 20 words for adult writing; in a sample of 10 sentences, aim for 9–10 different lengths and a bell-curve centered 15–18 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure syntactic pacing: include short 'punchy' sentences and some long ones for variety, but avoid making crucial points in overly long sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in sentence construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the same sentence template repeatedly (e.g., adverbial + subject + verb + object); use varied constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor sentence templates and avoid repetitive patterns; varied constructions improve readability and rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tight parallels purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Two adjacent sentences with exactly the same construction (tight parallels) are an effective way to communicate similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ parallels deliberately for emphasis and clarity rather than as an accidental habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic sentences are high literary forms; not typical in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic sentences (where grammatical and physical ends coincide) are high literary forms more appropriate for church or literature than technical papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of such forms, but avoid them in most technical exposition where directness is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control emphasis by sentence placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphatic positions are the front and the back of a sentence; recast sentences to change emphasis deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with sentence fronting and endings to highlight or deemphasize points; the middle of a sentence is less emphatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual labor techniques for close reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual techniques (typing or copying passages by hand, memorization, recitation) slow reading and help serious analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use copying, longhand transcription, or recitation to internalize rhythm and catch subtle problems; these techniques can improve attention to detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud and form critique partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and listen to each other; form partnerships to read drafts aloud and give feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud reveals awkward phrasing and rhythm; collaborate with peers but limit exposure to avoid fatigue from poor drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion and verse exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Scansion exercises and even writing verse can improve mathematical prose by sharpening sensitivity to rhythm and cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although unconventional, rhythm training can strengthen prose control—consider incorporating scansion exercises sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precis and compression practice
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot always reduce word count without changing structure; practice precis exercises to learn what to omit and how structure shifts with compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive compression to discover core structure and acceptable sacrifices in detail while preserving meaning where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ben Franklin-style rewriting from memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewriting a passage from memory with limited hints exposes differences in emphasis and clarity between original and your version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this exercise (preferably with admired writers' passages) to learn what makes an exposition effective and to internalize good phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a thesaurus and good dictionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone needs at least one thesaurus and a good unabridged dictionary; build vocabulary judiciously rather than hoarding big words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a nuanced command of common words and synonyms; consult reference works (e.g., Sidney Landau’s 'Dictionaries') to use words effectively.
